For the 0, 10, and 20 g per 100 mL sucrose solutions, the mass changes are +0.8 g, −0.4 g, and −1.3 g, corresponding to +8%, −4%, and −13% of the starting mass. Students can use the direction and size of these changes to consider which biological processes could explain the pattern.

-

Osmosis offers a plausible explanation for these results. Net movement of water across partially permeable cell membranes is from higher to lower water potential and could change the mass of the tissue. Weighing a cylinder does not show that movement directly, and differences in blotting or sample preparation could also affect a measurement. I would ask students which part of their account rests on the table and which part requires biological reasoning.

-

The change from mass gain at 0 g per 100 mL to mass loss at 10 g per 100 mL suggests that an intermediate concentration might produce little net mass change after 30 minutes. A near-zero change in tissue mass at that time would still be an indirect observation, rather than proof that the solution is isotonic with the cells. Without replicate samples, these data also cannot establish an exact concentration. Students could plot concentration against percentage mass change, then propose additional intermediate concentrations and repeated trials. They would also need to consider whether cylinder dimensions, potato source, and blotting procedures were consistent.
